utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I would like to briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the next witness be escorted into the courtroom, and, Ms. Hochhauser, your next witness is Mr. Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Celanovic, I take it. Mr. Celanovic, before you give evidence, the Rules require --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have to read it in other languages. Please be seated, Mr. Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll -- you'll now be examined by Ms. Hochhauser. Ms. Hochhauser is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find her to your right. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you please tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Zlatan Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, you have testified before this Tribunal previously in the Blagojevic, Tolimir, and Popovic trials; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And before coming to court today, have you had the opportunity recently to listen to your testimony in the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And after reviewing that testimony, can you tell us was the information that you provided in response to questions during that trial both truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would you give substantively the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And were there any answers that you felt you needed to correct or make any changes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would tender 65 ter 28863, which is relevant excerpts from that testimony in the Popovic trial and the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. Lukic? We'll start with the transcript. And, Mr. Registrar, transcript receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1451 is admitted into evidence. Associated exhibits, Ms. Hochhauser, could you go through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First would be 65 ter 04230, which is the Bratunac Brigade interrogation notes, dated 13 July 1995, of Mujo Husic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it will receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1452, Mr. Lukic, can I admit it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do have some problems with following the numbers. Give me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- you find them on the list of associated exhibits. The first one is grey, and then the next one ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If you're in need of another chart listing them, I can provide you with them, with another chart with the list of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Now I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections. P1452 is admitted into evidence. Next one, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1454, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1455, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1456, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And finally, 65 ter 14447.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1457, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may read a summary of the witness's evidence. I've informed the witness that what I say is not evidence only his testimony in evidence. Zlatan Celanovic is a lawyer who served during the war in the Bratunac Brigade under the command of Vidoje Blagojevic. In July of 1995, he was working in the moral, legal, and religious branch of the Bratunac Brigade. At times he worked with Captain Momir Nikolic, the Bratunac Brigade chief of security and intelligence. Sometime just prior to the 13th of July, 1995, Mr. Celanovic met with Ljubisa Beara, chief of the security administration for the sector for intelligence and security affairs. Beara ordered Mr. Celanovic to interrogate Muslims who were brought to him to see if they were in a book which listed Muslims purported to have committed war crimes. On the morning of 13 July 1995, Momir Nikolic brought Resid Sinanovic, a Bosnian Muslim lawyer from Bratunac who was a former colleague of Mr. Celanovic into Mr. Celanovic's office. Pursuant to this order from Beara, Mr. Celanovic spoke to Mr. Sinanovic about allegations against him but found the accusatory information unreliable. Five or six other Bosnian Muslim prisoners were also delivered to the brigade headquarters by soldiers, and Mr. Celanovic questioned all of them and took notes of the interrogation. After the interrogations, Sinanovic and the other Muslim prisoners were taken to one of the schools in Bratunac. That same afternoon, Mr. Celanovic observed transport vehicles, including trucks and buses, filled with Muslim men who had been taken prisoner. The evening of 13 July, Mr. Celanovic met Beara again, and reported to Beara that only a few people had actually been brought to the police building and there were too many Muslim prisoners in town. As a result, Celanovic and Beara proceeded back to the school, walking by the length of buses and trucks full of detained Bosnian Muslim men. Celanovic could see the men inside the school, and he watched Beara go down to the school and then look into the football stadium where Celanovic could see parts of buses and trucks within. And that concludes my summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hochhauser. If you have any further questions, you may put them to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could please have 65 ter 13594 on the monitor. Oh, I'm sorry, it has an exhibit number now which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise P1456 and the markings on it, which are a little bit difficult to see, in green pen, as having been marked by you previously in the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document. Is it possible to zoom in part by part? Well, now I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, because the markings in that green pen are a little bit difficult to see, I'm going to ask you some questions about the markings on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if we could perhaps have -- I don't know what colour is now available in the pen for the witness to make additional markings. If we could just make sure it's not green. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, first, before you mark anything, just let me ask you these questions. On the upper left-hand corner of what we now see on the screen, it looks like four -- what we see are four white kind of cylinders, and at the end of it there's a long green circle, or a long green rectangular shape. Do you see what I'm describing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, can --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see the circle, though. Maybe if we scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Actually, if we can leave it where it is. Do you see --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: A little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Do you see on the upper --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I recognise this facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us the long green rectangle at the end of -- that you've marked at the end of -- on the upper left-hand corner of the screen now, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a building where the command of the Bratunac Brigade was housed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, just underneath that marking there's a square in the green ink. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a gatehouse at the entry point to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, if you could with the pen that you now have just circle again with a circle and a square those two buildings that you've pointed out to us.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, can you please, sir, mark with an S the school which you and Mr. Beara walked to as described in your statement at -- the description is in the statement at pages 16 through 17 in e-court. Do you need us to zoom in on the map at all to make it larger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not possible. You will lose the markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Stewart has just informed me of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need for that. I can see it. Yes, I can see it. I can see it. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And, sir, can you put an S for "school."

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to direct -- I'm going to ask you a question now, and then we'll go back to the map. So if you can just put the pen down for a moment. Directing your attention specifically to the evening of 13 July when you walked with Mr. Beara into Bratunac such as you describe in P1456, your earlier testimony, and you approached the school, can you tell us were you able to see inside of the school, and, if so, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: One can see into the school from the street. It was possible to see people standing at the windows. In this particular case, those were the Muslims, captured Muslims, who were locked up or detained in the building of the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And were you -- could you also from your position out on the street hear anything from within the school?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one could hear something. People -- some people were standing at the windows. Some of them were shouting, "When are you going to let us go?" They were asking for water, most of them did, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Were you able to hear any responses given to those questions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no one to answer. There were only guards securing them, and they ignored their questions, comments, or whatever. That probably repeated itself by the hour, and they probably got fed up with providing them with answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, when you made those observations, both of what you've just told us you saw and heard from within the school, were you with Mr. Beara at that time? Was he with you when you saw and heard these things?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn back to the map that's on the screen again, and can you use the pen to mark where in relation to the school you and Mr. Beara stood when you made these observations? Can you tell us -- can you show us by marking -- by marking with a B, with the letter B, where you were.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, we see on the map a green line tracing from what you've marked again as the headquarters to the school, and you marked that in the Popovic trial as the path that you walked with Mr. Beara. And as we approach the school, we can see a number of Xs along that road leading up to the school. In the Popovic transcript, at e-court pages 27 to 28, it indicates that these Xs are the -- show the location of the buses that you saw with the Bosnian Muslim men. Can you show us on this map how long -- how far on this road where you've marked it that train of buses existed? So was it -- did it take half that street or all of the street? Can you tell us where you first saw them and where they ended?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the beginning until the end of the street but not along the entire line that you see here. Between Gavrila Principa Street and the school, and it covered the whole length as marked here. The street which used to be called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters didn't understand the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were buses everywhere. Maybe I can make it easier by showing you on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can put one X. Put the first X where you started seeing the buses, where you first noticed them, and put the second X where the line of buses ended, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, the interpreters had difficulties in catching the name of the school. Or the street, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And also if you could repeat, please, the name of the street where you saw these buses so that the interpreters can hear it.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Hacima Midhata Street it was called before the war. Now, what its name currently is, I don't know, because the municipality probably changed it as many municipalities did. I know that it was called as I mentioned, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And if you could mark the map with an X on the beginning of this -- on the part of the street where you first saw the buses and the second X where the line of buses ended.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: And the second X that you've drawn is around a curve, is that correct, onto a second street?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Did the length of buses go the entire way from the first X that you've marked, around the curve to the second?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The convoy was parked. It wasn't on the move. But in these side streets the vehicles were empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: So the location -- the buses that are in the location marked by the second X were empty. The buses on the street, the length of the first X that you marked, were those buses filled with people?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Now, just one last question for you. During this -- during this time period on the 12th and 13th of July, did you see or hear about anyone during this time period making lists of the Muslim men that were detained there, taking names or making lists of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard of anyone making such a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for the time. That concludes my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hochhauser. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I apologise. Ms. Stewart reminds me that I would like to offer the marked map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, the number of the map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1458, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1458 is admitted. Mr. Celanovic, you'll now be cross examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, colleague.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll start asking questions, and I will ask you about your work. During the war and after it, your tasks included, among others, the drafting of documents about the attacks of Muslim forces on the Serbian villages around Bratunac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I collected statements about those attacks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time you were qualified to do this kind of work, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you also co-operated with the commission for the investigation into war crimes of both Yugoslavia and of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander authorised you to take such statements. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All statements you collected you handed to one of these commissions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: To both.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your work, did you receive information about the number of Serb villages attacked in the area of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us not enumerate that, but tell me instead which percentage of Serb forces [as interpreted] in the Bratunac area was attacked by Muslim forces. Was it above 90 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: It was over 99 per cent. Only two villages were not attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking to people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm a little lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You started off asking about villages that were attacked. At page 14, line 13, you said: "Let us not enumerate that, but tell me instead which percentage of Serb forces --"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should be Serb villages. I didn't notice it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us repeat the question for the transcript. Which percentage of Serbs villages in the Bratunac municipality was attacked by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll answer differently. Apart from Polom and Slapasnica, all villages were attacked by Muslim forces in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many Serb villages were there in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 20 or 30. I don't have the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why I'm asking you this? Was it your impression talking to ordinary people that, among these ordinary people, hatred towards the Muslims was growing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: There was hatred towards the crimes on the part of those people who lost relatives. Certainly friendship wasn't thriving because war is war, and you always hate your enemy. You don't love him. It was the same on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you notice at the time that due to that hatred there was a growing desire for vengeance among fighters and others?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I sensed the desire for the war to end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the second sentence of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among the people, there was the desire for the war to end, just to end. There was no fanatic hatred or wish for vengeance. I didn't notice that among the Serbs or among the Muslims with whom I had contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us what were the consequences of the Muslim forces' attacks at Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly the same over and over again. There were killings, there was looting, and there was burning. At the end, the goods, including houses and everything, was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doing your work, taking statements from people and interviewing them, did you establish the identity of the persons who attacked the Serb villages and where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims who were staying at Srebrenica, but they weren't all originally from there. The attacks came from the direction of Srebrenica. There was a security line on their side and a security line on our side. Obviously they were coming from Srebrenica and withdrew there after the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did those attacks go on from 1992 until 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: They went on almost throughout the war, but they were the most intensive in 1992 and in early 1993. They were very frequent then. There was some periods without attacks, too, when everything was quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the attacks continue while Srebrenica was a protected area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now move on to your additional tasks. You assisted the work of -- assisted in the work of the investigative bodies; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You collected documents that had to do with war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also took part in inspecting convoys; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that those were not your regular duties?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: They were not. They were occasional duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And these additional duties were given to you by your commander?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You reported directly to the commander about these matters?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. If I did it, that meant that nobody else was allowed to do it. The chief was Momir Nikolic. The transport lists and the list of goods transported by convoys would later be given to Momir Nikolic, and he forwarded them to the commander. If he really did that, I don't know, but he certainly had archives of these lists that contained all information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't report to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the check-points around Bratunac functioned in accordance with the orders of the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you about Mr. Sinanovic. Do you know how Momir Nikolic and Mr. Sinanovic met?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know from the statement of Rasid Sinanovic. He told me that he had reported at the check-point or whatever it may be called, because I wasn't there, at Pobudje which is a village that belongs to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he moving with the convoy? I didn't quite understand that part?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not. He arrived on foot from Srebrenica. He came to the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. He went through the wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic handed him over to you; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: He brought him to the office and reported to me that he had brought him and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While he was in the office with you, nobody insulted or beat or mistreated Mr. Sinanovic in any way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: While Mr. Sinanovic was in the office with me, only I was present, and later we were joined by a friend of his who had asked to be admitted to see him. Only the two of us had contact with him, and God forbid that we beat him or did anything else to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nobody ordered you to insult or hurt him in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no one to give such orders, but even if so, it was my personal decision not to hurt anyone. That is my personal choice. Nobody can order me to do so -- or, rather, they could have ordered it, but I wouldn't have obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, Mr. Sinanovic was taken to the school, right, where the other detainees were?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The police drove him from my office to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Other people from Bratunac visited him there; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that only later. They were his neighbours or acquaintances, a couple of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These people who visited him at the school were also Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke to detainees twice with -- once with Mr. Sinanovic and once with others. Who did you inform of this fact?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't inform anyone, but I made a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did that note reach Major Jeftic or Commander Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Beara, he told you that you would be involved in the triage process, separating those who may have been responsible for war crimes from the others; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he told me what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you had a book entitled "The Chronicle of Our Cemetery," and that it contains information about which Muslim fighters from Srebrenica were found guilty of war crimes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D967, please. Can we get that from e-court. This is the very book, and we'll take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is not usual to conduct investigations based on books, but can we say that this book is one of the results of the investigations in which you also took part?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't call it an investigation. It was really a collection of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you collect that information? Could you give us an account in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: By taking statements of the surviving inhabitants of Serb villages that had been attacked. Many civilians had been killed, and defenders of the villages, and goods were destroyed. And then we also took statements from prisoners of war who were then exchanged. That is, Serbs who had been taken prisoner and then exchanged for Muslims, and even from the Muslim prisoners of war. We also got information out of them, who of their commanders and units had done what and where and when. Those were our sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in collecting the material for this book in one of its segments?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the book itself, your name is mentioned as one of the people working on it.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I remember having read it. There were quite a few of us who worked on the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you questioned witnesses, certain forms were used, and I'm talking about the witnesses, survivors from the Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this, the statements themselves were taken in this manner: The typist would type their statement as I would relate them. They would speak and I would make a summary of them, and at the end they would sign it. However, there was a general form for such situation, and I sometimes filled it out in order to know who the person who gave the statement was and what he says. And after I had collected a few such statements, I would hand them over to one of the commissioners who were involved in these investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the book itself deals with the chronological order of the attacks on the Serb villages, that it contains the names of the victims of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is also stated that it deals with the historical reasons. And speaking about the historical reasons, what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that among the people, irrespective of who they were, whether they were Serbs or Muslims, there was a long-lasting suspicion as a result of the consequences of the Second World War. Many more Serbs were killed during the Second World War in that area. Let me just give you one example. Our parents used to tell us that we mustn't forget the village of Obad [phoen] where a Ustasha unit obliterated the entire village and killed all its inhabitants. So all these things were happening also after the Second World War, after the First World War in particular, and there was a certain tension among the people, and this latent hatred was present even during the Communist era. It amounted to hatred and false friendships. Of course there were realistic and normal people on all sides. They just wanted to be normal human beings, whether they were Serbs or Muslims or whatever. Now, everything negative that happened had its roots in the Second World War, and it erupted, this unfortunate war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that many dead bodies exchanged with the Muslims or had been subsequently discovered in places where they had been killed, that many of these bodies were mutilated in a variety of ways?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were such instances. I personally didn't have an opportunity to see anything like that except on two occasions, once in the clinic when an examination was conducted or post-mortem was conducted. The bodies were handed over to the relatives in such a state. But there's another thing. I would rather speak about those who were alive. When they handed over our prisoners, they were totally beaten up, and they were barely alive. I know that for sure because I was obliged to question them and to take a statement of them asking them to describe how they had been treated by the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the physician who conducted the post-mortem examinations and forensic examinations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Dr. Veljko Macesic [phoen], and he was not the only one who carried out this. At the beginning of the war, once or maybe on a few occasions, there was Dr. Stankovic from Belgrade. I know, because I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me now move in time. Particularly let's go now to July of 1995, because I want to ask you this: At that time, did you hear that any of detainees was killed in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in July in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Can you please repeat your answer, because it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In July in the town of Bratunac, and I'm talking about that, I didn't hear of any killings of the detainees or of anyone being killed in the town for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. We're close to quarter past 3.00, which would complete the first hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And anyway, I'm moving to another topic so it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this perhaps is the right time for a break. Witness, could you please follow the usher. We'll take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we will resume at 25 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time. The Chamber has received a letter with suggestions from the Prosecution in relation to expert testimony - Mr. Lukic, I think you received a copy of that - asking for an administrative hearing or at least suggesting an administrative hearing on the matter. Do you intend to express your views on that as well or -- we haven't seen any response. It's not a formal motion but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Definitely we will have something to say on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when could we expect -- or would you like to do it orally or when do you intend to say something about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have nothing fixed yet, but I think that Mr. McCloskey mentioned something to me during this break, and we'll probably be able to inform you in couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes. Just for the parties to know that the Chamber, of course, is very much inclined to focus on the real issues in dispute, and if, for example, mistakes are made, that you identify the mistakes and that you agree that a mistake is made, rather than to go through all the details of many matters and rather focus on what really is important. But for the time being, we'll then hear from you as soon as possible, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My -- if I remember correctly, we filed something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't seen anything, but that does not mean that you have not filed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will check with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do that and we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- until then, perhaps you continue your cross-examination of the witness. Mr. Celanovic, it's not very polite to continue talking when you enter the courtroom, but we're in the middle of a short conversation. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On one of those days you headed off towards Potocari with some medical personnel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you reached the Yellow Bridge, Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we arrived at Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: As far Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whom you took to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I took Dr. Vesna Ivanovic and a nurse. I don't remember her name. They asked me simply to drive them up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you what was the reason of their visit?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to provide medical assistance if necessary, because there were a lot of people there, it was very hot, and that was what doctors do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, something relating to the issue of supplies of Bratunac. Was enough electricity provided to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there enough food?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After Yugoslavia imposed sanctions, did that contribute to the deterioration of the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any shortages of medication?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, something about the international humanitarian convoys. Is it true that several humanitarian convoys arrived in Srebrenica, many more than to Bratunac? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was approximately the ratio between the aid received by Srebrenica and the aid received by Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: It's easier for me to tell you in the numbers of vehicles. If a humanitarian convoy arrived in Srebrenica, let's say made up of 15 trailers trucks, only one or two or perhaps three would remain in Bratunac and the rest of them would go to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How well equipped were members of the Bratunac Brigade in terms of uniforms, weapons, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, the uniforms were made of very bad material. We had camouflage trousers and jackets, but due to the economic situation, it was bad. But as for weapons, it was pretty good. We had automatic, semiautomatic, and heavy weaponry as well. Now, whether that was sufficient or not, it was, in my view, given the number of soldiers who were in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me now ask you about the Dutch soldiers in Bratunac. In July 1995 you saw DutchBat members; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where in Bratunac did you see them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the military police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they taken prisoner? Were they armed? Can you give us an account?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think they were taken prisoner, because they were carrying their own weapons. They also had helmets, bags, and they had their weapons on their shoulders or in their hands. If they had been prisoners, they -- or if they had been taken to the military police building as prisoners, they should have been disarmed. That's why I think that they weren't prisoners but that they had crossed over to the Serb side. I'm positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they had crossed over to the Serb side? What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about an incident, but whether that was the real reason, I dare not venture to guess. But I heard that in one of the Srebrenica villages there had been an incident. I'm sorry. I apologise. Let me switch this off. I forgot. There was an incident when Muslim forces attacked a patrol or a unit of UNPROFOR, and on that occasion, an UNPROFOR soldier was either wounded or killed. I'm not sure about that. And that must have triggered their decision to cross over to the Serb side where they felt safer. That's not only my conclusion. That's when -- what the interpreters said to the military police commander, because neither him nor I speak English and couldn't speak to them without an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now about the attack on Srebrenica about which you testified elsewhere too. Do you know what the final reason was? What was the straw that broke the camel's back, and why was Srebrenica attacked although it was a protective zone?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I heard. In 1995, before the attack on Srebrenica, there was another raid of a Serb village, I don't know which village though, in the Vlasenica municipality or the Sekovici municipality, and there was the usual stuff, a massacre of civilians, looting, torching houses, at a time when that shouldn't have happened. There were international forces, it was a protected zone. And that was that proverbial straw. I cannot give any further comments because I don't know the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, before or after that, hear about the existence of a plan to expel the entire population of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard of such a plan, but I heard of something else, namely that the purpose was to disarm Srebrenica. That's all I heard before the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's return to Mr. Beara. We spoke about his saying to you that you should check whether there are war crime suspects among the prisoners. You were saying to him that it wasn't all right and that the town was at jeopardy; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beara told you at Bratunac on the 13th of July, 1995, that all prisoners would be exchanged at Kladanj on the following day; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that moment, were you waiting for the buses and trucks that had taken the women and the children away to return?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So there weren't enough vehicles to transport all the men to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Beara told you when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- and now let's jump back to 1992. Do you remember when the first fighting started in the Bratunac municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Around the beginning of June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to remind you that the first victims fell on the 3rd of May, 1992, and the surrounding villages, would that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certain about July. I even know some dates. Everybody from Bratunac knows about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, I mean 1995, I'm now back at Srebrenica, you didn't see General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I only saw him once in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: When the Bratunac Brigade took part in the liberation of Slivansko Brdo or Zeravica, because I was also sent up there as a member of the command with soldiers and I took part in the fighting up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. 1993 or 1994, possibly. I would hate to give you a wrong date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, speaking about the men who had set off from Potocari on buses, how were they separated from the women and children? Who took them out of the buses?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how that was done. Probably they informed everybody, using megaphones, that women and children and the elderly could leave separately because the people had to know how to -- how to group, how to form groups. I wasn't up there, so I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know you weren't up there. You also mentioned that lists of people who had come to Bratunac were not made.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was supposed to make these lists at Bratunac? Who was tasked with that? Should Momir Nikolic have organised it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if lists were supposed to be made. I never thought about that, because I was always convinced that they were being taken to Kladanj and why make lists.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unused microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether that's part of Momir Nikolic's remit. Anyway, nobody made lists. If they had been made, I would know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Colonel Savo Sokanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Zeravica village, do you know where that is?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: On Romanija, close to Pijanovac. I don't know what the nearest town is, probably Sokolac, or possibly Han Pijesak. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, since you were there, do you know that, in 1992, Colonel Savo Sokanovic's father was killed in that village in?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic was your superior?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He wasn't?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he authorised to assign you tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I received my tasks from the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How would you describe Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: How should I describe him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I mean as a person, not physically.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: When he was doing well, he was rather arrogant. When he wasn't doing well, then his mood would vary. He was a difficult person. I don't know how to sum him up, but he didn't treat me badly, nor did I treat him that way. When he needed assistance, expert assistance, he would let me know, but he never showed an inclination to do anything that was outside the usual rules of warfare, and that includes the treatment of prisoners. He always treated prisoners fairly. I'm now speaking about the previous years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are drawing to an end. Just let me check if I have any more questions. At a certain point --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Celanovic, these were all the questions I had for you. Thank you for replying to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser, do you have any questions on re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour, just maybe two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, on cross-examination you were asked at temporary transcript page 29 about Mr. Beara's statement to you that the prisoners would be exchanged at -- would be exchanged the next day but that there were -- you were waiting for buses and trucks. And I'm just drawing your attention back to that question and answer. Was Mr. Beara with you when you saw the empty buses and trucks that you described to us earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could just ask your indulgence to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I may have one or two questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you took a doctor and a nurse to Potocari. You took them there. What was the reason for you to go there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The only reason was the fact that I had a car, and I happened to be in front of the clinic, and they asked me for a ride because there was no way for them to get to Potocari, which is 7 or 8 kilometres away after all. That's the only reason I went up you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you familiar with what other -- what persons in the Military Police Brigade were doing during those days? Your task was that you had to interview persons, I do understand, that were brought to you. Did you have any idea about what your colleagues, police officers, did during those days?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: They were securing the officers in the field, they were securing prisoners, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would they take prisoners? Would people surrender to them or ...

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, people did not surrender to them. They just guarded the people who came to Potocari, and they acted as security officers while escorting the officers. Normally they did not take part in taking prisoners. They were not a unit engaged in the field that would be actively involved in any operations on the ground, so their role was to provide security both for the prisoners and our officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They would not be active in apprehending persons, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard from members of the military police, that they were not actively involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from what you heard, is there any other basis for your answers, because before you said -- you said, "They were securing prisoners, and that would be it." Then you said, "No, people did not surrender to them." Did you have any basis apart from what they told you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any other basis. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Because I wasn't in the field, and therefore I wasn't able to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but, for example, you went to Potocari. You passed at Zuti Most. You didn't see any of your colleagues there, or did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Let me explain Potocari and what it means when I went there. First I came to a building that belonged to the electric company, and some 100 metres away I saw a small cordon of members of the DutchBat, and they were actually the last line that the people from Potocari could go. And I also saw many buses who were waiting to receive people. I did not cross that line. I did not have any reason to go and mix with the crowd. It is possible that they were either there or elsewhere, but I did not see them. And the reason I didn't see them was that as soon as these two ladies alighted from my car, I turned it and I went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I have no further questions for you. None of the parties has further questions for you. Mr. Celanovic, this -- unless there's any -- the questions by the Bench have triggered any need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Mr. Celanovic, have you heard -- did you hear that Mirko Jankovic, the military police platoon commander, went up and down the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road in a UN APC and called out for the Muslims to surrender? Do you know that? On the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that fact. He was the only one who knew how to drive this particular vehicle and that he was riding along that route, but whether he was calling people to surrender, I don't know. I did not hear any fact about that. I know that this APC was used to go to Konjevic Polje and to Kravica and back, and that vehicle belonged to the DutchBat. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hochhauser. This, then, Mr. Celanovic, concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for come the long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two questions for the parties in this context. Ms. Hochhauser, the witness testified that he had listened to the transcript -- to the audio and that there was no need to make any changes. Of course, we have to work with the transcript. Could I take you to page 6635 of the transcript, the original numbering. I don't know what page it is in e-court. Second line from the bottom. "A. Not in that sense. I did thought mention the 28th Division, and I didn't know there was a 28th Division. I asked him whether he -- that I did thought mention." I had some difficulties in fully understanding it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I suspect it would be "though" with an added -- an extra T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes ... now, I've been thinking about that as well, and then my next thought was: If you think that you have mentioned the 28th Division and you didn't know whether that existed, that comes as a surprise slightly, because why would you mention something you are not aware of that it exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: What I can do, Your Honour, is have a B/C/S listener listen to the original audiotape for that -- at that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Lukic, I think you introduced the book, "The Chronicle of Our -- Chronicle of Our Graveyard," 1D9 -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked it be on the screen. I don't know what you want to do with it. Leave it as it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe the best way is to MFI it, since this book will probably be used, for example, with the next Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you hardly used it now. We can also leave it. The reason why I'm raising the matter, because I would have left it, you introduced as the book, where it seems to be excerpts of the book. Is that -- at least I see page -- this one, it's jumping from one page to another. So if you want to use it in the future, then perhaps take care that we know exactly what it is that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Then we leave it for the time being, so 1D967 doesn't receive any number at this moment. I am looking to the Prosecution. We will have to take a break, but I wonder whether it's of great use to use another 25 minutes for the next witness and then get in some trouble anyhow time-wise for the remainder of the day, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe we have a witness available before the videolink. This took a little less time than we anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear. That is true for both parties. Then I will use the time for a few matters. I first would like to deliver an oral decision. I'm just checking whether the booths have received a decision. I'll deliver the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's request to substitute Witness RM044 with a new witness. On the 16th of April, 2013, the Prosecution confidentially filed a motion seeking leave to add a new witness to its Rule 65 ter list as proposed Rule 92 bis witness, in substitution of proposed Witness RM044. Due to the fact that the Prosecution has not yet assigned a particular witness number to the witness, the Chamber only refers to it as the "new witness" for the purposes of this decision. The Prosecution submits that Witness RM044 was to provide evidence in relation to the alleged massacre at Grabovica school including in the indictment as scheduled incident A.8.1, but the witness passed away in 2012, before providing a witness statement satisfying the requirements of Rule 92 quater. On the 30th of April, 2013, the Defence filed its response submitting that it does not object to the Prosecution's motion. The Chamber notes that the subject matter of the evidence of both witnesses concerns the alleged killing of a number of men in or around Grabovica school on or about the 3rd of November, 1992. The Chamber, so as to clarify, points out that the evidence in question relates to scheduled incident A.4.4 of the indictment and not as mistakenly referenced by the Prosecution in its motion, scheduled incident A.8.1. Considering the inability of the Prosecution to present the evidence of Witness RM044 as a result of this witness having passed away and taking into account that the Defence does not object to the requested substitution, the Chamber, pursuant to Rule 65 ter, grants the motion and instructs the Prosecution to file full information in relation to the new witness as required under the said Rule. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Then I would like to address the parties, but more specifically at this moment the Prosecution, on the following matter: In the context of the testimony of Peter Boering on the 18th of April, the Chamber expressed concern with the practice by the Prosecution to deviate on a more frequent basis from the stated preference by the Chamber to receive Rule 92 ter evidence through statements rather than transcript excerpts. It alerted the Prosecution to the fact that it would consider how to proceed in this regard. This is to be found at transcript page 10003. Upon admission of the 120 pages of transcript excerpts of Peter Boering on the 19th of April, the Chamber noted that it may not be so lenient in the future. The Chamber accepts that tendering transcript excerpts rather than statements is in specific cases justified. With respect to transcript excerpts that are longer than approximately 50 pages, however, the Chamber would like to urge the Prosecution to file such motions at least four weeks in advance of a witness's expected start of testimony so that the Chamber is in the position to consider whether it would not perhaps be in the interests of judicial economy to hear such a witness viva voce or, as the case may be, leave the Chamber with enough time to request the Prosecution to take a statement for the witness in question as opposed to tendering the lengthy transcript excerpts. The first witness for whom the Chamber shall make this consideration is Mirko Trivic, who is expected to start his testimony on the 21st of May, 2013, and for whom there are 80 pages of previous testimony being tendered. The Prosecution is urged to review the 80 pages tendered for Mirko Trivic to ensure that it cannot further be reduced. In this regard, the Chamber has noted that for several witnesses who recently testified, subject matter discussed in detail in the tendered transcripts are then also elicited orally from the witness during the examination-in-chief. This should be prevented so as not to waste court time. Then the last item I would briefly address is about MFI D285. Exhibit D285 was tendered into evidence through Mile Janjic on the 10th of May and subsequently marked for identification pending provision of a revised B/C/S version. And you can find this at transcript pages T 11061 and 11062. The Chamber has been informed by the Prosecution that a revised version of D285 has been uploaded in e-court under 65 ter number 4205A. The Chamber hereby requests the Registry to replace D285 with 65 ter 4205A and admits D285 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I make one correction of the transcript. Line 12 of page 41, the page should be 11062.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we still hope not to end up in the 121.000s. This now being on the record, I think we will resume, let's say, a couple of minutes before 5.00 so that we can start at 5.00 sharp. We'll then further hear evidence in closed session today. We resume at five minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To hear the evidence of the next witness, we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Do I understand, Mr. Shin, that you have no witnesses for tomorrow before 5.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to permit Mr. McCloskey to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have any witnesses -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, my simple question is: You have no witnesses tomorrow before 5.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The simple answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any witnesses tomorrow before 6.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any witnesses for the day after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can I refer this to Mr. Lukic from now on? No, I'm just kidding. Yes, we have the two Srebrenica survivor women that are arriving late tonight that will be ready to go on Thursday. Though, like other witnesses last week and this week, we're finding both the Prosecution and the Defence are taking less time and their estimates are getting smaller, and as a result, we're getting -- we're getting some gaps. I would like to think we're reaching a rhythm where we're not contesting things that we thought were contested and I think I'll even give the guidance some credit for this, though it is creating gaps that we're trying rapidly to make up. But we could finish both women on Thursday or likely the -- Friday morning, and we don't have anyone that we can bring in Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No way to start tomorrow already at 6.00 for, let's say, for one hour? I don't have the estimates for these witnesses on my mind. I don't know how vulnerable they may be in arriving and then starting their testimony already the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- that might be possible. We usually like to give them a day to adjust. One of them has never testified before. The other has testified before but is sensitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know how much time. Again, I don't have the estimates here at this moment. I then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would like to leave it in the hands of the parties what is wisest to do. If that would mean that we would start the witness only -- the witnesses only on Thursday, then the Chamber accepts that. We expect the witnesses starting on Thursday, two witnesses remaining, to finish their testimony this week, and if possible, even on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's looking very possible as I'm seeing the new estimates that are coming in. We have 30 minutes for one of the women and the other wouldn't be much longer, and I know their estimates are shorter. So we could very well finish on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic is still hopeful, but not fully convinced yet. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because my colleagues are actually cross-examining those witnesses, Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Ivetic. So I'm not sure about Mr. Ivetic's estimate. I know Mr. Stojanovic's estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we adjourn for the day, and we will resume -- although we first will turn into closed session. We'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 15th of May, at 5.00 in the afternoon in this same Courtroom III, if I'm not mistaken. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of May, 2013, at 5.00 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
